summary: Recommends a practice for revoking posting rights to IETF mailing lists for people who engage in bad faith disruption. It gives the IETF a way to manage participant interaction when a person attacks its consensus process. It is a best current practice that has been replaced by RFC 9945.

eli5.summary: If one person keeps shouting and breaking up a meeting, the group needs a fair way to ask them to leave. This explains how to take away someone's right to post. RFC 9945 replaced it.

subtitle: How the IETF can remove a disruptive person's right to post to its mailing lists.

tldr.problem: A small number of participants have disrupted the IETF's consensus-driven process by repeatedly posting off-topic or inflammatory messages to its mailing lists.
tldr.mechanism: The IESG may approve a new kind of action, a PR-action, that removes named people's posting rights, using its normal last call and consensus steps.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3683 has been replaced by RFC 9945, and it was also updated by RFC 9245.

today: RFC 3683 is a Best Current Practice that has been replaced by RFC 9945. It was also updated by RFC 9245.

sections.title: Why the IETF Needed a Practice
sections.content:
The IETF develops standards through a consensus-driven process, and mailing lists are central to it. Unlike many organizations, anyone may post to an IETF mailing list. For this memo, an IETF mailing list means any list under IETF auspices, including the general discussion list and working group or design team lists.

In a small number of cases, a participant has mounted what amounts to a denial-of-service attack on the process, typically by repeatedly posting messages that are off-topic, inflammatory or otherwise counter-productive. The RFC separates this from good faith disagreement. A working group that fails to reach consensus is acceptable, but one that is continuously disrupted is a case of abuse. In the memo's words, individual bad faith should not trump community goodwill.

Existing guidelines already cover abusive behavior, and in practice have included temporary suspension of posting rights, with longer suspensions each time. When that does not work, the memo offers a more drastic measure.
sections.eli5: Most people who disagree in a meeting are fine, and that is healthy. Someone who keeps interrupting on purpose so nobody can finish is a different problem.

sections.title: The PR-action
sections.content:
The IESG already makes decisions called actions, such as publishing a standards-track document or chartering a working group. This memo adds a new one, the PR-action (posting rights action). It names one or more people and cites messages they posted to an IETF mailing list that appear abusive of the consensus-driven process.

If the IESG approves it, the named people lose their posting rights to that list, and maintainers of any other IETF mailing list may also remove their posting rights at their discretion. The action stays in force until explicitly nullified and SHOULD stay for at least one year. After a year a new PR-action MAY be introduced to restore the rights, and the IESG SHOULD consider how often such requests come. If rights are restored, the person must contact the list owners to get them back.
sections.eli5: The leaders can vote to stop a person from posting, and the person has to wait at least a year before the leaders can vote to let them back in.

sections.title: How a PR-action Is Decided
sections.content:
Whether the action revokes or restores rights, the IESG follows the same steps it uses for other actions:

  1. An IESG Area Director introduces it, and may first inform the interested parties.
  2. It is published as an IESG last call on the IETF general discussion list.
  3. The community discusses it.
  4. The IESG discusses it.
  5. The IESG decides, using the usual consensus-based process.

As with all IESG actions, the appeals process in RFC 2026 can be used to contest an approved PR-action.

Working groups SHOULD keep their lists manageable. Someone might try to dodge a revocation by changing email address, so it should be possible to restrict the new address.
sections.eli5: The decision goes through the same fair steps as any other big decision: someone proposes it, everyone gets to talk, and the leaders decide. The person can still appeal.

sections.title: Limits, Security and the Q&A
sections.content:
A PR-action deals solely with posting rights. Consistent with RFC 2418, no action may be taken to prevent individuals from receiving messages sent to a mailing list.

The Security Considerations section says this memo deals with matters of process, not protocol, and notes that it describes a mechanism to throttle active denial-of-service attacks on the consensus-driven process.

The appendix is a short Q and A. It argues that a year is not too long because a PR-action is approved only after substantive consideration. It says a single action should cover all IETF lists, since requiring one per list would enable a prolonged series of attacks. It also says IESG actions are formally started by an Area Director even though the motivation usually comes from outside the IESG.
sections.eli5: The person can still read the messages, they just cannot send new ones. The rules are about how people behave, not about computer settings.
